questions.question_text: A student reports $57\times403=22\,971$. Which estimate best checks the answer?

options.text: $6\times400=2\,400$, so the answer is too large
options.why: Rounded fifty-seven to six, losing one place-value position.

options.text: $60\times40=2\,400$, so the answer is too large
options.why: Rounded four hundred and three to forty, losing one place-value position.

options.text: $600\times400=240\,000$, so the answer is too small
options.why: Rounded fifty-seven to six hundred, adding an extra place-value position.

questions.solution_text:
$57\times403\approx60\times400$
$=24\,000$
$22\,971$ is close to $24\,000$, so it is reasonable.

questions.question_text: Which judgement of $1\,284\div6=214$ is supported by estimation?

options.why: Lost a place-value position when dividing twelve hundred by six.
Moved the place value in the wrong direction, making the quotient exceed the dividend.

options.text: Impossible, because division answers cannot exceed $100$
options.why: Applied a false size rule; a quotient may be greater than one hundred when the dividend is large.

questions.solution_text:
$1\,284\div6\approx1\,200\div6$
$=200$
$214$ is close to $200$, so it is reasonable.

questions.question_text: A learner writes $76\times298=2\,264$. What does $80\times300=24\,000$ show?

options.text: The answer is about $10$ times too small
The answer is about $10$ times too large
options.why: Reversed the comparison between two thousand two hundred sixty-four and twenty-four thousand.

options.text: The answer is reasonable because both begin with $2$
options.why: Compared only the first digit instead of the place value and overall magnitude.
Lost two place-value positions from the benchmark product twenty-four thousand.
Lost one place-value position; thirty-five hundred divided by seven is about five hundred.
Added a place-value position, making the quotient larger than the dividend.
Used a two-digit quotient even though thirty-five hundred divided by seven is in the hundreds.

questions.question_text: Since $31>30$ and $247>240$, what must be true of $31\times247$?

options.why: Reversed the effect of increasing both positive factors above thirty and two hundred forty.
Treated the rounded benchmark as the exact product rather than a lower estimate.
Added an extra zero to the benchmark product thirty times two hundred forty.

questions.solution_text:
$30\times240=7\,200$
Both original factors are larger, so $31\times247>7\,200$.

questions.question_text: The product $392\times70$ is reported as either $2\,744$ or $27\,440$. Which answer has a reasonable magnitude?

options.why: Lost the zero contributed by multiplying by seventy rather than by seven.
Added an extra zero beyond the one contributed by the tens factor seventy.
Used a nearby-looking value but reduced the hundreds contribution without a valid multiplication step.
